q: What unexpected genetic cargo has the flowering shrub Amborella accumulated inside its mitochondria?
a: DNA from other kinds of plants
d: Its mitochondrial genome contains large amounts of foreign DNA, including material from mosses and green algae. These transfers crossed branches of the plant family tree rather than following ordinary parent-to-offspring inheritance.
s: Rice and colleagues · Amborella mitochondrial genomes
choices: A complete bacterial chromosome replacing its mitochondrial genes
DNA only from its own chloroplasts
DNA from other kinds of plants
Extra copies of all its nuclear chromosomes
evidence: Primary abstract reports foreign mitochondrial DNA from green algae, mosses and other angiosperms, including whole-genome transfers.

q: Cardamine chenopodiifolia hedges its reproductive bets by making fruits in which two places on the same plant?
d: Its aerial fruits explode and scatter seeds. Separate underground fruits remain non-explosive and contain fewer, larger seeds, keeping some offspring near the parent’s successful site.
s: Max Planck Institute · Amphicarpic development
choices: On its leaves and its roots
evidence: Institutional study account contrasts aerial explosive fruits and underground non-explosive fruits formed from buried self-pollinating flowers.

q: Where have researchers shown brewing yeast can spend the winter and then pass to a new insect generation?
d: Overwintering social-wasp queens carried Saccharomyces cerevisiae from autumn to spring and transmitted it to offspring. An insect gut can connect yeast populations across seasons.
s: Stefanini and colleagues · Wasps and yeast ecology
evidence: Experiment demonstrated yeast persistence in adult overwintering Vespa and Polistes queens and transmission to progeny.

q: In germination experiments on Suaeda aralocaspica, how did its fresh brown and black seeds differ?
a: Brown seeds were ready; black seeds were dormant
d: Brown seeds in the study were ready to germinate, while black seeds showed physiological dormancy. Producing both types spreads the risk of committing every seed to the same opportunity.
s: Wang and colleagues · Dimorphic desert seeds
choices: Both colors germinated immediately at the same rate
Brown seeds were ready; black seeds were dormant
Both colors needed freezing before germination
Black seeds were ready; brown seeds were dormant
evidence: Primary experiment found brown seeds nondormant and black seeds with physiological dormancy; seed types differ in germination behavior.

q: What can a dried-out fairy-ring champignon mushroom do when rain returns?
d: Marasmius oreades fruiting bodies can shrivel during dry weather and expand again after becoming wet. This drying-and-rehydrating behavior has earned it the nickname resurrection mushroom.
s: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew · Fairy-ring champignon
choices: Stay shriveled while new mushrooms grow nearby
Shed its cap and grow a replacement
evidence: Kew account explicitly describes complete drying followed by expansion and regained shape after rain.

q: Some fungus-farming ants maintain helpful bacteria on their outer bodies. What service do those microbes provide?
d: The bacteria produce compounds that suppress fungi attacking the ants’ crop. Specialized body structures and glands help support this microbial defense.
s: Currie and colleagues · Ants’ bacterial housing
choices: Sugars to feed the fungal crop
Nitrogen fertilizer for the cut leaves
evidence: Primary abstract describes antibiotic-producing bacteria in ant cuticular crypts supported by glands; related primary study PMID21106596 confirms defense against Escovopsis.

q: Leaf-cutting ants add fecal droplets to fresh leaves in their gardens. What useful material do these droplets recycle from the fungus they eat?
d: Fungal enzymes survive passage through the ants and reach newly cut leaves. They help break down plant material for the growing fungal crop.
s: Rønhede and colleagues · Fungal enzymes in ant gardens
evidence: Primary experiment identifies cell-wall-degrading enzymes of fungal rather than ant origin in fecal droplets.

q: The dyes in traditional litmus paper were extracted from what living material?
d: Several lichens supply the dye mixture used to distinguish acidic from alkaline solutions. A familiar laboratory indicator therefore has a biological source.
s: EMBL–EBI ChEBI · Litmus
evidence: ChEBI chemical database defines litmus as a mixture of dyes extracted from several lichen species. Botanical garden account independently corroborates source.

q: What human-made debris has been found tangled in Mediterranean seagrass fiber bundles called Neptune balls?
d: Wave-worked Posidonia fibers can trap pieces of plastic and carry them ashore. Researchers measured this natural trapping process in material washed onto beaches in Mallorca.
s: Sanchez-Vidal and colleagues · Seagrasses trapping plastics
evidence: Primary paper examines microplastics and larger plastic pieces in beached seagrass material; university release explicitly describes incorporation into fiber balls.

q: In a landmark Arizona murder investigation, DNA from which overlooked plant material helped connect a vehicle to the crime scene?
d: Palo verde pods found in a truck were compared with trees near the body. The plant evidence challenged the suspect’s account of where the vehicle had been.
s: National Institute of Justice · Plant DNA evidence
evidence: Official forensic training account identifies palo verde seedpod molecular identification linking suspect to particular crime scene.

q: How does the fungus Entomophthora muscae help infected female housefly corpses spread infection to healthy males?
d: Fungal infection changes the dead female’s chemical signals. Males attracted to attempt mating can pick up infectious spores from the corpse.
s: Naundrup and colleagues · Fungus-driven fly attraction
choices: Making them imitate a rival male
Making them release a swarm alarm
evidence: Primary study links fungal volatile blends and altered host hydrocarbons to male sexual attraction and infection.

q: The ants living with Nepenthes bicalcarata can do what inside the plant’s fluid-filled pitchers?
d: Camponotus schmitzi ants swim in the pitcher liquid and retrieve food. Their partnership with the carnivorous plant includes food, shelter and services that help the plant capture or process prey.
s: Clarke and Kitching · Swimming ants and pitcher plants
evidence: Primary study describes swimming ants hauling prey from pitcher fluid and consuming it.

q: Why can temporarily ineffective, dry pitcher-plant traps eventually catch more ants than continuously slippery traps?
d: Experiments supported a model in which dry rims let scouting ants visit safely. Later wet conditions make the surface slippery when a larger recruited group arrives.
s: Bauer and colleagues · Temporarily inactive pitcher traps
choices: Ants lose their grip as nectar ferments
Dry pitchers raise the temperature of entering ants
Dry rims concentrate salt that slows ants
evidence: Primary experiment and model support safe access for scouts promoting recruitment; framed as can, not deliberate planning.

q: Why can’t ordinary seed-bank drying and freezing preserve many oak acorns?
a: They cannot tolerate that much drying
d: Such seeds are called recalcitrant. Researchers instead explore carefully prepared tissues and cryopreservation methods, because treating whole acorns like dry grain can kill them.
s: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew · Cryopreservation
choices: They need constant exposure to light
Their shells prevent them from cooling
They lose all their starch when chilled
They cannot tolerate that much drying
evidence: Kew states recalcitrant seeds die when fully dried and whole frozen acorns suffer lethal ice formation.

q: What unexpected growing position helped Kew propagate the tiny waterlily Nymphaea thermarum successfully?
a: On wet mud exposed to air
d: The breakthrough came from copying its hot-spring-edge habitat. Seedlings improved when kept at the surface of wet soil instead of being submerged like typical waterlily seedlings.
s: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew · Nymphaea thermarum
choices: On a floating mat of dry leaves
On wet mud exposed to air
At the bottom of deep warm water
On damp bark above the water
evidence: Historical cultivation account reports surface-level water and air exposure producing mature flowering plants; no current extinction-status claim.

q: The long twining part of a Lygodium climbing fern may look like a vine stem. What is it actually part of?
d: Its frond’s central axis can keep extending and coil around supports. The climbing structure is an unusually long-growing leaf rather than the main shoot of a flowering vine.
s: Mueller · Shoot morphology of Lygodium
evidence: Primary morphology paper describes indeterminate leaves with shootlike continuous growth and circumnutation; Smithsonian flora corroborates twining frond axes.

q: What holds some lodgepole-pine cones shut for years until sufficient heat allows their seeds to escape?
d: In serotinous cones, resin bonds the scales together. Heat can melt that bond, releasing stored seeds after a fire has opened space for new seedlings.
s: National Park Service · Fire and lodgepole pine
choices: A layer of wax plugging each seed
A tight web of woody fibers
A pressure difference inside the cone
evidence: NPS describes cones sealed tightly with resin that melts during fire; scoped to some cones because serotiny varies.

q: Researchers proposed that pale patches on Caladium steudneriifolium leaves deter egg-laying moths by resembling what?
d: The variegated patches look like mines left by feeding larvae. Experiments with natural and painted markings supported the idea that appearing already attacked can discourage new attacks.
s: Soltau and colleagues · Defensive leaf variegation
choices: Reflections from droplets of sticky sap
evidence: Primary study tests mine-like variegation and finds reduced herbivory; question preserves proposed interpretation.

q: What unusual process clears away the aging gills of the mushroom Coprinus comatus as its spores mature?
d: Its cap progressively breaks down into a dark, spore-bearing fluid. Dissolving older tissue helps expose the remaining spore-producing surfaces.
s: Australian National Botanic Gardens · Mushroom spore discharge
choices: Peeling off as a dry membrane
evidence: Botanical garden account describes cap dissolving into an inky mess and dripping away; progressive tissue removal assists spore escape.

q: The white patches on a typical red fly-agaric mushroom cap are leftovers from what?
a: A covering around the young mushroom
d: The universal veil surrounds the developing mushroom. As it expands, pieces of that covering can remain as patches on the cap.
s: University of Wisconsin–Green Bay · Amanita descriptions
choices: A covering around the young mushroom
Clusters of spores released through the cap
evidence: University descriptions identify cap patches as universal-veil remnants; does not provide mushroom-eating guidance.

q: Some dramatically streaked tulips prized during Dutch tulip mania owed their patterns to what unexpected cause?
d: Tulip breaking virus can disrupt flower coloration, creating contrasting streaks. A visually prized pattern could therefore be a symptom of disease.
s: Royal Horticultural Society · Tulip viruses
evidence: RHS ties tulip breaking virus and flower breaks to seventeenth-century tulipomania; not all striped modern tulips are infected.

q: During its heat-producing flowering phase, what does a sacred lotus do when the surrounding air becomes colder?
d: The flowers can keep a relatively steady warm temperature across large environmental changes. Measurements show stronger metabolic heat output as ambient temperature falls.
s: Seymour and Schultze-Motel · Lotus thermoregulation
choices: Keep heat output fixed regardless of air temperature
Let flower temperature track the air without compensation
evidence: Primary abstract reports proportional increase in heat production as air cools and relatively stable flower temperatures; active regulation distinct from simple heating.

q: Bubbles can emerge from the center of a lotus leaf where water has collected. What internal process causes them?
d: A canal system sends pressurized air through leaf stalks and submerged rhizomes. Gas can vent through central leaf pores, producing visible bubbles if water covers the outlet.
s: Matthews and Seymour · Lotus gas canals
choices: Fermentation by microbes in pooled water
Oxygen released by algae growing on the leaf
Dissolved gas escaping as pooled water warms
evidence: Primary anatomy article describes gas bubbling through pools on lotus leaves and pressure-driven gas transport. Companion primary DOI10.1111/pce.12163 details leaf–petiole–rhizome ventilation.

q: Some fern colonies survive far beyond the range of the familiar leafy plants. Which living stage can make up these colonies?
d: The small sexual generation can live independently and spread vegetatively. Its distribution may extend far beyond that of the recognizable, spore-producing leafy generation.
s: American Fern Society · Independent fern generations
evidence: Society account describes independent fern gametophyte populations beyond sporophyte ranges and species without known sporophytes.

q: In Charles and Francis Darwin’s grass-seedling experiments, shading which small region could prevent bending toward light?
d: Opaque caps over the tip greatly reduced bending even when the lower shoot remained illuminated. Removing the caps restored the response, separating light detection from the growth response farther down.
s: Charles Darwin · The Power of Movement in Plants, pages 471–474
evidence: Read primary1880 text pages471–474: opaque upper caps prevented or greatly reduced Phalaris bending; transparent caps did not; removing opaque caps restored response. Not a universal no-bending result.
